pending.title: Soldier receives Bronze Star for Valor for ‘fearless actions’ after drone strike at start of Iran war
pending.summary: The Army recently published a series of photos of an award ceremony for a soldier credited with saving lives following an Iranian drone strike on U.S. troops in Kuwait at the start of the Iran war. Sgt. 1st Class Oscar M. McGrew was awarded a Bronze Star with “V” device for valor during an Oct. 23 award ceremony at Fort Hood, Texas. The images, which were uploaded on Oct. 26 to the military’s image database , mark one of the rare instances in the ongoing conflict where an enlisted soldier has received the award for valor. Task & Purpose was the first to report that Sgt. 1st Class Oscar M. McGrew had been recognized for his response during the March 1 Iranian one-way drone and ballistic missile attack on Port Shuaiba, Kuwait. The attack was part of a series of Iranian retaliatory strikes on American bases around the Middle East in the opening hours of the war. The strike killed six Army Reserve soldiers and injured more . To date, it remains the deadliest of the war. The Army confirmed to Task & Purpose in September that McGrew was the Directorate of Logistics noncommissioned officer-in-charge for Area Support Group-Kuwait. Sgt. 1st Class Oscar McGrew, center, during the award ceremony at Cooper Field on Fort Hood, Texas, Oct. 23, 2026. Army photo by Spc. Michelle Lessard-Terry. Captions for the photos of the award ceremony identify McGrew as a member of the 215th Brigade Support Battalion, 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team. “His fearless actions directly saved lives and prevented further casualties during an active enemy attack,” the photo caption reads. When the Army confirmed McGrew’s award to Task & Purpose in September, officials said additional details of the Kuwait attack would not be released until the families of the six soldiers who were killed in the incident received an official 15-6 command investigation brief. Inquiries sent to the Army for details of McGrew’s now-public award were not immediately returned on Thursday. McGrew is credited with taking direct action that saved lives following the Iranian drone strike. Army photo by Spc. Michelle Lessard-Terry. The Pentagon has released minimal information on the toll that the Iranian attacks have taken on U.S. troops. The details contained in personal awards, particularly in their citations, narratives, and speeches during award ceremonies, are one of the key ways that the media and the public can get a sense of the challenges and risks service members are facing in America’s latest conflict. Task & Purpose was the first to report that the military services had awarded just over 202 Purple Hearts to troops injured in the Iran war as of mid-October. One of those soldiers was Army Reserve Lt. Col. Robert J. Connolly, who was, as of last month, still recovering from his injuries at a Soldier Recovery Unit at Fort Bliss, Texas . According to the Pentagon’s public-facing casualty database, 23 service members have died while deployed in support of the Iran war . Eleven were killed in hostile incidents, and 12 were classified as non-hostile deaths. According to the Defense Department, 867 troops have been injured in combat operations against Iran. pending.title: Israeli parliament erupts in chaos as Netanyahu bloc loses vote
pending.summary: Israel's deeply divided parliament descended into chaos on Wednesday as lawmakers traded insults, hurled accusations and shouted over one another, exposing bitter political divisions after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's far-right bloc suffered its first defeat in the newly elected Knesset. The confrontation erupted during the inaugural meeting of the Arrangements Committee, where extreme-right lawmaker Tally Gotliv was forcibly removed from proceedings after repeatedly interrupting fellow legislators, according to Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth . Committee chairman Roy Folkman, from former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, ordered Gotliv, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's extremist Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to leave as tensions escalated. Gotliv continued shouting and protesting as she was escorted from the room, while Palestinian lawmakers chanted "Out, out", according to the Israeli newspaper. The disorder followed a significant political setback for Netanyahu, whose bloc lost a parliamentary vote on the committee's composition by 63 votes to 50. The proposal, backed by Eisenkot's bloc and Palestinian lawmakers, marked the first defeat for Netanyahu's allies since the October 27 Israeli elections, which left the prime minister, who is now serving in a caretaker capacity, without a parliamentary majority. Insults and bitter exchanges The committee meeting quickly deteriorated into a shouting match as lawmakers exchanged personal insults and accusations. Newly elected Likud lawmaker Erez Tadmor was branded a "weapons thief" by female legislators, referring to his previous conviction for stealing military equipment during his army service. Tadmor, who was sentenced to 45 days in prison over the offence, responded by calling lawmaker Merav Ben-Ari a "hen", triggering accusations of misogyny. He then attacked Eisenkot's bloc for cooperating with Palestinian parties, repeating accusations that they supported terrorism. "This is my second day in the Knesset and I am shocked," Tadmor said, according to Yedioth Ahronoth , before accusing rival lawmakers of rejecting Netanyahu's calls for unity. Tadmor also called Democrats lawmaker Naama Lazimi a "roadblocker", prompting her to respond sarcastically: "There is your unity." This was apparently a reference to Netanyahu's calls for a "national unity" government excluding Arab parties following the election. The confrontation escalated when Gotliv repeatedly interrupted Lazimi as she criticised the treatment of lawmakers and families of Israelis killed or taken captive during the war. Gotliv accused Lazimi of mocking Netanyahu's appearance, prompting another heated exchange before Folkman ordered her removal. Despite the chaotic proceedings, the committee approved the appointment of Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman to chair the temporary Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee. Liran Avisar Ben-Horin was also appointed to lead the temporary Finance Committee. Netanyahu attacks Palestinian lawmakers The clashes highlighted the growing divisions in Israeli politics as Netanyahu struggles to retain power following an election that denied his far-right bloc a governing majority. Palestinian parties have emerged as important players in the parliamentary arithmetic, with their support helping Eisenkot's bloc secure its first victory. Netanyahu has repeatedly attacked Palestinian lawmakers while simultaneously calling for a national unity government under his leadership. During a speech on Tuesday, he accused Palestinian parties of supporting "terrorism" and condemned Eisenkot's bloc for negotiating with them. His remarks prompted Eisenkot's Yashar party to cancel planned coalition talks with Likud, accusing Netanyahu of delivering a divisive speech. On Wednesday, Netanyahu renewed his appeal for unity, declaring that Israelis must come together in the face of security challenges. Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed the appeal but warned against forming a government reliant on Palestinian parties, urging Eisenkot to reach an agreement with Netanyahu instead. Meanwhile, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that Netanyahu was attempting to prevent the newly formed Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee from convening in the coming days. The committee is responsible for parliamentary oversight of Israel's military and intelligence agencies, including the authority to question senior security officials. The political turmoil comes ahead of a November 17 vote to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, in another test of his bloc's dwindling parliamentary influence. Eisenkot is continuing negotiations to form a government, with the latest confrontations underscoring the hostility between rival Israeli factions and the central role Palestinian lawmakers could play in determining Netanyahu's political future.

pending.title: Houthis deny targeting Mecca amid Saudi missile interceptions
pending.summary: Yemen's Houthi movement has denied targeting Mecca after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted drones heading towards Islam's holiest city, while debris from two ballistic missiles fell in parts of the surrounding province. The Saudi-led military coalition said on Wednesday that its air defences had destroyed three cruise missiles headed towards Riyadh and two drones launched towards the Mecca and southern regions of Saudi Arabia. It also reported intercepting two missiles directed towards the west of the kingdom. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree rejected the allegation that the group had attempted to strike Mecca, describing the Saudi account as false and insisting that Houthi operations were directed at oil infrastructure and military installations. Saree said the group had instead launched a drone attack against an oil pumping station in Yanbu, on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, and fired three cruise missiles at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi authorities did not confirm an attack on the Yanbu facility. The competing claims about the intended targets could not be independently verified. Early on Thursday, Saudi civil defence reported a separate incident involving two ballistic missiles it said had been launched towards the Mecca region and intercepted by Saudi air defences. Saudi state television identified two places where debris fell: Sabuhah village, approximately 35 kilometres northeast of the Grand Mosque, and Wadi al-Maghmas, about 21 kilometres east of the mosque. Saudi civil defence called the alleged targeting of civilian sites a violation of international humanitarian law. The Houthis had not issued a specific response to the latest report of falling missile debris by early Thursday, although they have repeatedly denied targeting either Mecca or Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam. Mecca is home to the Kaaba and the Grand Mosque and is the destination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Allegations that it has been deliberately targeted have particular religious and political sensitivity across the Muslim world. Renewed fighting across Yemen The latest Saudi-Houthi war of words comes amid intense fighting in Yemen following the September breakdown of the truce that had largely frozen the conflict since 2022. The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, say their missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia are retaliation for Saudi attacks on areas under their control. Riyadh has intensified air strikes against Houthi positions, while the group has attacked or claimed attacks against airports, oil facilities and military installations. Saudi air defences also reported intercepting missiles aimed at Riyadh on Tuesday. An attack on King Khalid International Airport last month killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Reuters . On Sunday, an attack attributed to the Houthis damaged a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Riyadh. Fighting has also continued inside Yemen. Forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, claimed on Wednesday to have killed or wounded 138 Houthi fighters in attacks across several provinces, while the Houthis said they had struck a Saudi-backed military command facility in Aden's al-Buraiqa district. Neither side's battlefield claims could be independently verified. The human cost is rising. The World Health Organisation said fighting had killed 2,098 people and wounded 9,657 as of 8 November, while more than 320,000 people had been displaced since the beginning of August. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the strategic passage connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

pending.title: How Israel's occupation is swallowing Syrians into its prisons
pending.summary: Israeli forces have seized Syrian civilians from their homes and farmland, transferred them to a detention system notorious for its treatment of Palestinians, and left families searching for relatives whose whereabouts remain concealed, a new investigation has found. The Syria Justice and Accountability Centre’s (SJAC) report, Taken in the Night , draws on 23 interviews, field monitoring and open-source research to document arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance and treatment amounting to torture in several cases. It places those abuses within Israel’s expanding occupation of southern Syria following Bashar al-Assad’s fall in December 2024. Salma Daoudi, SJAC’s research and policy officer and the report’s lead author, told The New Arab that the arrests served purposes extending beyond individual interrogations. "I think that these detainees themselves have become leverage," she said, warning that their fate was becoming entangled with negotiations over Syrian territory and sovereignty. The UN Commission of Inquiry, in findings presented in September this year, identified 49 individuals, including two children, who had been detained by Israeli forces on Syrian territory. Israel has occupied the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967. After Assad’s overthrow, its forces seized the UN-monitored buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement and advanced into further parts of Quneitra and western Daraa, establishing ten military positions. Israel describes its deployment as temporary and denies that it constitutes occupation. SJAC, however, concludes that its effective control over parts of southern Syria triggers the obligations of an occupying power, regardless of how Israel characterises its presence. The report documents the establishment of ten military positions, as well as military roads, checkpoints, restrictions on access to farmland, home demolitions and displacement alongside the arrests. These measures have progressively undermined residents’ ability to move freely and sustain their livelihoods. Daoudi said Israel increasingly treated the occupied Golan and newly seized Syrian areas "as one operational territory", folding southern Syria into its wider security framework. The detention practices, she argued, demonstrated an effort "to really exercise direct and indirect forms of control over the population". Arrests as a means of control SJAC documented arrests of shepherds, farmers and children, including a 14-year-old who was detained while tending sheep. Other civilians were taken during pre-dawn raids involving large military forces, dogs and drone surveillance. Witnesses described men being stripped, children held at gunpoint and families' phones being confiscated. One woman reported suffering a miscarriage shortly after her husband’s arrest, which she attributed to the distress caused by the raid. Some operations appeared to have been planned around detailed information about particular households. Former detainees described interrogators using photographs and satellite imagery, which Daoudi described as "extremely worrying". "[Israel] even knows the barber that the person goes to, for instance, which shows the extent of its stronghold and command of the information." While questioning focused on alleged connections to Hezbollah, Iran and Russia, other arrests occurred as civilians carried out ordinary activities . Daoudi said this unpredictability itself imposed restrictions on daily life. "Some of them are really terrorised and very worried because of this arbitrariness that I think is really designed to cement and project control." The report traces three detention routes: confinement at military positions inside Syria, transfer to Sde Teiman inside Israel, and onward movement into Israeli Prison Service facilities, including Ofer in the occupied West Bank and Nafha and Negev prisons. For their families, those transfers can mean months without official confirmation of a relative’s whereabouts. Some have only managed to obtain their first information through released Palestinian prisoners, lawyers or human rights organisations. Torture and detainees used in military exercises At Sde Teiman, former Syrian detainees described being stripped of their names and assigned numbers, forced into stress positions, threatened with firearms and subjected to stun grenades. Their accounts mirror abuses previously documented against Palestinian detainees at the facility. One man interviewed by SJAC described interrogation about supposed connections inside Syria. "I had no such knowledge, but that made no difference," he told investigators. Among the most disturbing allegations is the use of detainees in Israeli military training exercises, including simulated arrests and hostage-rescue operations. "They’re using the detainees as stunts, or as props," Daoudi said. She stressed that such treatment served no interrogation purpose, describing it as "using detainees and humiliating them further". pending.title: UK Selects Norwegian P1118 Design for New Mine-Hunting Motherships
pending.summary: The Royal Navy will acquire three Offshore Support Vessels—with options for three more—to operate uncrewed mine countermeasure systems and support NATO’s northern flank as part of the wider UK-Norway Type 26 partnership. UK MoD press release UK and European security will be bolstered by a new Royal Navy commitment to acquire three new mine-hunting motherships. Under the deal, the UK will buy three new ships which will act as motherships for uncrewed mine-hunting systems, boosting UK security by making the detection and disposal of sea mines safer, quicker and more effective. An additional £90m investment was announced in the Defence Investment Plan for the acquisition. The agreement between the UK and Norway supports the export of Type 26 Global Combat Ships to Norway, the UK’s biggest-ever warship export deal by value, which supports 4,000 jobs across the UK supply chain, including more than 2,000 at BAE Systems’ Glasgow shipyards. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his Norwegian counterpart, Tore O. Sandvik, confirmed the UK’s commitment to the programme at the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo today, further strengthening the two nations’ shared commitment to tackling security threats. The vessels are a key step in building the Hybrid Navy and a major step in the UK’s defence partnership with Norway. They will be central to the Royal Navy’s modernisation of its mine-hunting capability, keeping sailors further from danger and supporting anti-submarine warfare capabilities on NATO’s northern flank. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said: This deal strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy. By using the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War to put the latest modern technology in the hands of our Sailors, we are helping to keep them safe and ensuring they have the tools to protect our shores. This agreement also shows how the UK-Norway partnership helps both our countries, and our allies, meet the challenges of a more dangerous world. The Royal Navy will receive the first of three Offshore Support Vessels in 2031, known as “standardised vessels” in Norway, with an option to buy an additional three vessels. The threat from Sea Mines has been brought into sharp focus following Iran’s illegal mining of the International Strait of Hormuz, which has caused major disruption to the global trade in energy. Acquisition of the globally deployable Offshore Support Vessels will ensure the UK stays at the forefront of safeguarding international freedom of navigation from fast-evolving mine threats. The agreement will see the UK join Norway’s major naval programme, the P1118 Standardised Vessel Programme. Norwegian Defence Minister Tore O. Sandvik said: The United Kingdom’s procurement of Norwegian Standardised Vessels will further strengthen our strategic partnership, rooted in the Lunna House agreement. Operating similar platforms will enhance our navy-to-navy cooperation and further improve our ability to operate seamlessly together, protecting and safeguarding NATO’s northern flank. Alongside Norway’s £10 billion procurement of Type 26 frigates in December 2025, the new agreement means the two navies will operate similar ships, strengthening interoperability between two close NATO allies. The Offshore Support Vessels will be delivered through the government-to-government Maritime Capability Partnership Framework (MCPF) between the UK and Norway. The announcement was made at Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo, where further maritime and industrial commitments were also highlighted. These include Arondite’s £35 million investment over five years to open an Oslo office and grow its European operations. Atlantic Net, a £90 million contract awarded by the Ministry of Defence and Royal Navy to Ocean Infinity , will combine autonomous and uncrewed systems with advanced sensors to detect and monitor underwater threats across the North Atlantic. Discussions among allied navies were held through the International Sea Power Conference (ISPC), convened by the First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins. pending.title: Israel to launch military strikes without opposition approval
pending.summary: Israeli caretaker Defence Minister Israel Katz said Thursday that the outgoing coalition does not need permission from the opposition to decide on fresh military operations, following calls to show restraint. "We do not need approval from the opposition or any legal authority" for the army to carry out strikes in any of the arenas where it operates, Katz wrote on X. His comments came as the Israeli military killed at least 10 people in Gaza in the deadliest strikes since Israel's election last month. The leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot , has called on caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to show restraint, warning that the use of force without a "direct and immediate threat" could have "disastrous consequences for Israeli democracy and for citizens' trust". Netanyahu repeatedly threatened to resume the Iran war on the campaign trail for elections last month, warning of threats and even posting an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv. Katz said Thursday that the outgoing coalition had "demonstrated resolve and sound judgement in dealing with Iran, in full coordination with the IDF -- and that will remain the case now, as circumstances require". Netanyahu agreed to meet Thursday with Eisenkot to discuss national security following the row over whether the outgoing government can resume the conflict. In a short joint statement, Eisenkot and Netanyahu said they would meet at the prime minister's office for a briefing attended by Netanyahu's military aide. The announcement came a day after Eisenkot, who has a mandate to try to form a new government, accused Netanyahu of refusing to brief him, in what he called a deviation from protocol. Avigdor Liberman, a key member of Eisenkot's political bloc who has been named head of a parliamentary committee on foreign and defence affairs, also criticised Netanyahu on Thursday. "I warn you: a caretaker government is not allowed to make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full consent of all security agencies," said Liberman, a hawkish former aide to Netanyahu who has become a strident critic. Neither Liberman nor Eisenkot mentioned Iran directly. Netanyahu's office has hit back, saying Wednesday that Eisenkot, a former military chief, was politicising national security. Since last year Netanyahu has twice ordered major bombing campaigns against Iran in partnership with US President Donald Trump. Both leaders said afterwards that they had severely set back Iran's efforts to build nuclear weapons, which the clerical state denies pursuing. Trump has allied himself with Netanyahu but in recent days has said the focus is on diplomacy, after he also suffered a setback in elections, partly due to the war. Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, although President Isaac Herzog can give him an extension until 20 December. Both Eisenkot's broad left-to-right coalition and Netanyahu's bloc of hard-right and religious parties fell short of a majority in Israel's October polls. Eisenkot is exploring options to form a government, with Liberman demanding he not work with Israeli-Arab lawmakers, whose numbers soared in the elections on the back of anger over Netanyahu. Last year, rights groups EKO and the Irish Centre for Civil Liberties (ICCL) filed a complaint with Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), raising concerns that Microsoft’s Grange Castle data centre was hosting elements of the Almunasseq app , used by the Israeli army to monitor Palestinians. The DPC has still not given a definitive response to the rights groups over the status of the complaint. Sinead Gibney, who serves in the Dail Eireann, the Irish parliament's lower house, said Microsoft's Irish data centres are "fuelling the crime of apartheid against Palestinians" in the West Bank and Gaza. “Microsoft must be held accountable and I’ll be pushing for the Department of Enterprise to fully investigate this matter in light of the wealth of UN reports detailing the apartheid system," she told Middle East Eye. The complaint was submitted on behalf of a Palestinian resident of Gaza and the West Bank, as well as a European Union citizen, based on evidence provided by a whistleblower. Evidence seen by MEE and gathered by EKO and the ICCL showed that Israel used Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing platform to host elements of the Almunasseq app. According to the complaint, Microsoft provides the “underlying” and “essential computer infrastructure” needed for the app to function, including cloud storage, database services and computing power. This means information collected from Palestinians using the app could be processed and stored on Microsoft’s infrastructure. Whistleblower evidence submitted with the complaint also showed that parts of the app are hosted in Microsoft’s data centres in Ireland, potentially bringing them within the scope of EU data protection laws. The evidence was submitted to the DPC, which did not respond to MEE’s request for comment. Microsoft also declined to comment. pending.summary: François Picard is pleased to welcome the President of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric. “War may be a human condition. But barbarity is not”: The Red Cross warns of a dangerous erosion of the rules of war War may be an enduring feature of human history, but its brutality is neither inevitable nor beyond restraint. That distinction lies at the heart of a stark warning from Mirjana Spoljaric, President of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), who argues that the international rules established to protect civilians are being progressively weakened amid proliferating armed conflicts, technological transformations and the retreat of diplomacy. “You may consider war a human condition,” Spoljaric tells France 24. “But brutality, barbarity, is not a human condition.” Her warning recalls the fundamental premise of the 1949 Geneva Conventions: even in war, there can be no lawless space, and certain red lines must never be crossed. Yet from Gaza and Ukraine to Sudan and Yemen, Spoljaric describes an increasingly permissive interpretation of international humanitarian law, in which civilian infrastructure is attacked, populations are displaced and human suffering becomes an instrument of military strategy. “So humans are instrumentalized in the pursuit of military objectives,” she observes. The proliferation of drones and artificial intelligence adds another troubling dimension. Technologies once presented as instruments of greater military precision have not, she argues, delivered the promised protection for civilians. Instead, they risk further diminishing the possibility of escaping violence, while the prospect of autonomous weapons targeting human beings raises urgent legal and ethical questions. But Spoljaric's deepest concern extends beyond the battlefield. As conflicts increasingly cross borders and humanitarian needs overwhelm available resources, diplomacy itself appears to be retreating. Her message is ultimately political: humanitarian assistance cannot substitute for the prevention of war, and the protection of civilians cannot depend on goodwill alone. The responsibility, she insists, belongs to governments and citizens alike. “As a citizen, demand that your government prioritize the rules of war,” she urges, warning that “wars are coming to your doorstep nowadays much, much faster than in previous years.”

pending.summary: The Air Force is buying new helmets for fixed-wing aviators that are said to be lighter, better ventilated, and more adaptable to new technology than the current helmet — the HGU-55/P — that’s been in use for more than 40 years. On Nov. 5, LIFT Airborne Technologies announced it was awarded a 10-year contract with the Air Force for its AV2.2 Next Generation Fixed Wing Helmet system. The contract is worth up to $83.4 million and up to 16,000 helmets, which would be more than enough for all the commissioned fixed-wing aviators in the active-duty Air Force. And Air Force spokesman told Task & Purpose that the service expects deliveries of the helmet to begin in late summer 2027, with the goal of reaching initial operational capability that September. The one fixed-wing community not included in the contract are F-35 fighter pilots, who have their own brain buckets that cost about as much as a Ferrari . All other fixed-wing aviators have worn the HGU-55/P since the 1980s . But times are changing, and the Air Force said it needs different gear to help aircrew stay healthy and to keep up with new technology. That said, it is not clear at this time which units will receive the helmets first. Pain in the neck The HGU-55/P weighs about 2.2 pounds. That may not sound like much, but the pounds add up in high-G maneuvers. A human head weighs about 10 or 11 pounds. That plus a two-pound helmet, plus the weight of any attached heads-up displays or night-vision goggles, and it totals about 120 pounds sitting on the pilot’s neck in a 9G turn. Top Stories This Week News First female Marine elected to Congress as women veterans hit ‘record’ numbers By Patty Nieberg News Family sues Air Force over daughter’s brain injury from birth overseas By Patty Nieberg News The Army wants more pilots to apply for its special operations helicopter regiment. Here’s why By David Roza Not all maneuvers are that aggressive, but over time the strain forces many fighter pilots out of the cockpit. A 2019 medical study reported neck pain as a significant health problem affecting 51% of fighter pilots, of whom 39% reported time lost from flying. According to a LIFT fact sheet , the basic variant of the small- and medium-sized AV2.2 weighs 1.95 pounds, while the large and extra-large versions weigh 2.01 and 2.19 pounds, respectively. It’s not just the weight, but the center of gravity that counts, and the new helmets are designed so that night-vision goggles, targeting systems , and other gadgets balance better on a pilot’s head to reduce strain. Maj. Brett Gedman, 301st Fighter Squadron, brings down the Next Generation Fixed Wing Helmet’s visor prior to an F-22A Raptor mission March 24 at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida. Air Force photo by Samuel King Jr. Point of view One F-22 pilot raved about the AV2.2 when he flew with it in 2023. “The design of the helmet allows for unparalleled visibility, mobility, and comfort in the cockpit,” Maj. Brett Gedman said in an Air Force press release at the time. “The increased visibility combined with the mobility … made it a massive improvement over what I am used to flying with. It is clear this has been a generational leap in technology that the fighter pilot deserves, which is long overdue.” One enlisted support airman liked the new helmet, too. With the HGU-55/P, support airmen had to use power tools to add mounting brackets for night vision goggles and new heads-up displays. The AV2.2 is modular, so they can just swap out mounting attachments and pop on the new gear. That flexibility should also help as new technology comes online. “From a pre-flight and build-up standpoint, the new helmet is much better,” Airman 1st Class Matthew Crouse, an aircrew flight equipment technician, said in the 2023 release. The new headwear also has a moisture-wicking helmet liner and vents in the back so crew members’ heads don’t become sweaty swamps: a problem several pilots encountered with the older helmets , they told Task & Purpose in 2021. The Air Force’s Next Generation Fixed Wing Helmet sits ready for another testing at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida. Air Force photo by Samuel King Jr. There is still development left to go as LIFT fine-tunes the AV2.2’s attachments for mounting heads-up displays and other gadgets. It was also not immediately clear exactly how many helmets the Air Force plans to buy, or which aircrews will receive them first. Todd Lentz, chief revenue officer for LIFT, told Task & Purpose that the number of helmets delivered over ten years will depend on a number of factors, such as the population of pilots, the size and make-up of the aircraft fleet, and the cost per helmet. Questioned in parliament on Wednesday, Berendsen said diplomatic discussions were taking place but he would not specify whether proposals to shield national leaders and restrict the court's jurisdiction were under consideration. The exchange followed a report by Dutch rights organisation The Rights Forum , citing anonymous diplomatic sources in New York, that the Netherlands was negotiating restrictions in response to US sanctions. Hanneke van der Werf MP, from the Democrats 66 party, asked whether discussions included immunity for heads of state and government, excluding nationals of countries outside the court's founding treaty from its jurisdiction, and weakening its ability to intervene when national authorities fail to prosecute. Berendsen's answers did not confirm the reported proposals, but nor did they answer whether the government would reject them. "Discussions are currently taking place about the diplomatic track being pursued," Berendsen replied. "I cannot anticipate which subjects are or are not on the table." He added that the Netherlands could not decide the matter alone, because more than 120 member states would potentially have to reach an agreement with the US. 'All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking' – Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen "So the minister is not denying that it is true," Van der Werf responded. "All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking," Berendsen said. ICC member states are scheduled to meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December, after the session was relocated from New York because US sanctions and visa restrictions threatened participation. Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution on 9 October, escalating a campaign that had already targeted most of the court's judges and prosecutors. The sanctions have been imposed since February last year, in the aftermath of the arrest warrants issued by the court for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza . In the institutional sanctions, Washington granted a six-month exemption for certain operational transactions to allow time for negotiations, with its expiry on 7 April next year. Under the Rome Statute’s general amendment procedure, adoption requires consensus or a two-thirds majority, followed by ratification by seven-eighths of member states before entry into force. pending.title: Air Force aims for year-round operations at three Pacific islands
pending.summary: The Air Force intends to use four airfields in the Pacific for more than 6,000 aerial operations per year, as part of its expanding operations in the region. Calling it a “unique opportunity” to support new operational objectives, the Air Force plans to use Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport, all located in the Northern Mariana Islands, for thousands of training flights and aerial exercises per year. The operations are meant to support the service’s Agile Combat Employment, or ACE, strategy, which aims to disperse aerial operations over several locations to avoid creating one large target. The plan was announced in a notice of intent published late in October. The notice calls for getting environmental impact statements on plans to stage aircraft on the three Pacific islands. Top Stories This Week News An A-10 named ‘Rainbow Warrior’ sports Marilyn Monroe door art in the Middle East By Nicholas Slayton News Blue Angels aviator removed from team before homecoming show By Nicholas Slayton News The Army wants more pilots to apply for its special operations helicopter regiment. Here’s why By David Roza According to the notice, the Air Force wants to carry out up to 1,200 fixed-wing and 320 rotary-wing aircraft operations each year per airfield, or more than 6,000 in total annually. To support that, the service would set up temporary infrastructure at each airfield, which would each be staffed by up to 1,000 people. The islands are relatively close to each other and a few dozen miles away from Guam, which has become central to U.S. military planning on potential littoral and island-hopping campaigns in the Pacific. Per the Air Force, the plan would allow it to “test and employ tailorable force packages; exercise movement, sustainment, logistics, and command-and-control functions across multiple locations to replicate the complexity of distributed operations in contingency environments; and strengthen interoperability with Joint, allied, and partner forces within the Mariana Islands region.” There is also an alternative proposal, which could see even more aircraft flights from the four airfields and would allow for “up to 1,400 fixed-wing operations and up to 384 rotary-wing operations per airfield annually.” Draft environmental impact statements are expected next fall. The Air Force has been working to revitalize the airfields at Tinian for the last several years, upgrading infrastructure or in the case of the island’s North Field, clearing “overgrown jungle” to make the installation usable again. The airfields have been used in recent years, as part of multinational exercises like Valiant Shield, but not on the scale proposed here. The Air Force isn’t alone. Other branches have looked to old World War II-era bases in the Pacific as staging grounds for island operations. The Marine Corps has been rehabilitating a historic airfield on Peleliu . Additionally, the overall military has been expanding defenses and bases on Guam , which Air Force documents called “centralized operating installations.” The post Air Force aims for year-round operations at three Pacific islands appeared first on Task & Purpose .

The research found that users received no adequate explanation of which policy they had allegedly violated in around 70 percent of documented cases. pending.title: Maldives moves to pass unconditional ban on Israeli tourists
pending.summary: The Maldives is seeking to pass a law that would officially ban Israelis from visiting the island nation on a permanent basis, according to a statement from the office of President Mohamed Muizzu. The announcement of the bill was made at a press conference on Monday. "The current bill provides for an unconditional ban on entry for anyone holding an Israeli passport, irrespective of changing circumstances," the announcement from Muizzu’s office said. The archipelago of about half a million people previously passed legislation banning Israeli passport holders from visiting amid the war on Gaza, where Israeli strikes have continued despite an October 2025 ceasefire. The new bill would tighten these restrictions rather than introduce a first-time ban on Israeli travellers, which came into effect in April 2025. The existing restriction remains in force while the new proposal awaits parliamentary approval. The bill has so far passed its first reading in parliament. According to the president’s statement, the travel ban applies only to people entering on Israeli passports and does not extend to Israelis travelling on a second passport. In December 2023, Israel issued a travel warning advising its citizens against visiting the Maldives, citing rising anti-Israel sentiment during the Gaza war. The Foreign Ministry said Israel could have difficulty assisting them if they encountered trouble there. The Maldives lifted a previous ban on Israeli tourists in the early 1990s and briefly moved to restore relations in 2010. Separately, the Maldivian government has submitted a bill that would bar Israeli citizens and Israeli-owned companies from acquiring leasehold rights in designated development zones. Buyers would be subject to screening, according to local media reports. Unlike the travel ban, these restrictions would also apply to Israelis using a second passport. Muizzu described Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide , according to the president’s office, and said allowing Israeli passport holders into the country was unacceptable. Both bills still require parliamentary approval. The Maldives, a small country comprising 1,192 strategically located coral islands, is known for its secluded white-sand beaches, shallow turquoise lagoons and Robinson Crusoe-style getaways. Its population is nearly all Muslim.

pending.title: Palestinian journalists faced 134 Israeli violations in October
pending.summary: Israeli forces and settlers were responsible for at least 134 reported violations against Palestinian journalists and media institutions last month, with the occupied West Bank city of Hebron the worst-affected area, according to a new report published on Thursday. The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate’s Freedoms Committee's report details 134 crimes, attacks and violations against Palestinian journalists and media institutions in October 2026. The incidents were mostly committed by Israeli forces and settlers but also involve Israeli military courts. According to the committee’s monthly report, the violations included measures intended to obstruct journalists' work and restrict their ability to cover events. These included detentions, reporting bans, arrests, harassment, threats and raids on journalists’ homes and media institutions. Detentions and restrictions on media coverage accounted for the largest number of incidents, with 70 cases, followed by 27 incidents involving tear gas and stun grenades. The report also documented eight raids on journalists’ homes and media institutions, seven arrests and an equal number of cases in which journalists were referred to military courts. The report also highlighted physical attacks against Palestinian journalists, documenting three cases of journalists being wounded by live ammunition, one of whom was also injured by missile shrapnel. It further recorded five attacks by Israeli settlers. In addition, three journalists were subjected to questioning, while two cases involved threats and incitement. One journalist was also handed a financial fine. Hebron recorded the highest number of violations, particularly detentions of media crews, restrictions on coverage and the use of tear gas and stun grenades against journalists. These incidents took plac e amid an 11-day Israeli siege on the city , which resulted in the mass displacement of Palestinians. Last Tuesday, Al Jazeera reported that its correspondent Montaser Nasser had been arrested during an Israeli raid on his home in Dura, near Hebron. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reported last month that Israeli forces had also detained reporters, fired tear gas and directed lasers at news crews during a major raid in Hebron, describing the incidents as part of “escalating violence” against the media. CPJ added that these incidents followed a series of violations by Israeli soldiers and settlers targeting Palestinian and international journalists in the occupied West Bank, particularly while they were covering the ongoing olive harvest , which has seen a series of attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinian farmers. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) reported that at least five journalists and media workers had been arrested by Israeli forces or attacked by Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank since October. It said the incidents reflected a wider pattern of violence, intimidation and repression targeting local and international journalists reporting in Palestine. Since the beginning of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza on 7 October 2023 , Israeli military violence against journalists has escalated, with 24 times as many journalists killed and three times as many detained, according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF). RSF has described Israel as one of the world's ten largest prisons for journalists for the fourth consecutive year.

pending.title: British Army signs landmark pact with UK halal meat giant
pending.summary: The British Army has signed an agreement with one of the UK and Europe's largest halal meat suppliers to support military veterans, encourage British Muslims to join the Armed Forces and strengthen ties with South Asian communities. Major General Karl Harris and Tariq Sheikh, the British-Pakistani businessman and founder of Tariq Halal Meats, signed the Armed Forces Covenant at the company's headquarters in Wembley, west London, on Armistice Day on Wednesday. Under the agreement, the company will guarantee job interviews to former military personnel, provide reservists with paid leave for annual training and offer flexible working arrangements to partners of serving personnel. The company will also display the covenant in its shops alongside messages encouraging customers to join the Armed Forces. Sheikh said more than three million customers visit the company's shops each year. "This is your country and this is your Army," Sheikh told young British Pakistanis, encouraging them to join the military, its reserves or cadet organisations. The Armed Forces Covenant is a national commitment to ensuring that those who serve or have served in the British Armed Forces, along with their families and the bereaved, are treated fairly and do not face disadvantages in accessing public or commercial services compared with other citizens. Harris praised the historic contributions of South Asian soldiers from British India during the First and Second World Wars and their role in defending Britain. "We celebrate the history and heritage that we all share, whether that's the British Army or people from South Asian heritage," Harris said. "My maternal grandfather served in the Indian Army in Burma, and your relatives similarly served in that same theatre of war." Sheikh, who was born in Gujrat in Pakistan's Punjab province, also highlighted the longstanding military connections between Britain and South Asia. "For a hundred years Jhelum sent its sons into the British Indian Army," he said, referring to the Pakistani city where his wife was born. "The Pakistan Army was born of that same Army in 1947. Its regiments, its discipline and its pride are an inheritance from the British Army, and it has honoured that inheritance ever since." Sheikh said the agreement would encourage younger generations of British Pakistanis to consider military service. "Serve in it, join its reserves, send your children to its cadets, and carry the tradition on," he said. Thaira Sheikh, the company's chief financial officer, said anyone leaving the Armed Forces who applied for a job at Tariq Halal Meats would be guaranteed an interview. "Our reservists will have paid time for their annual training, and the partners of serving personnel will have flexibility when a posting comes," she added. Kunal Patel, the company's chief executive of franchises, said serving personnel, veterans and their families would be welcomed at its outlets, while franchise partners would support local cadet units and observe an annual moment of remembrance. Tariq Halal Meats was founded in 1994 in Southall, west London, and has since expanded into one of the country's leading halal meat businesses. Halal meat refers to meat from animals slaughtered and prepared in accordance with Islamic dietary laws derived from the Quran and Sunnah. In Arabic, halal means "permissible" or "lawful". According to the British Army's website, more than 450 Muslim personnel serve in the Army, while broader government figures indicate that Muslims account for approximately 0.4% of the UK's Regular Forces. The Muslim population in the UK is estimated at around four million, representing approximately 6% to 6.5% of the country's population, according to the Muslim Council of Britain.

pending.title: Netanyahu ally approached Mansour Abbas over Israel coalition
pending.summary: Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas has confirmed that a close confidant of Benjamin Netanyahu contacted him about the formation of Israel's next government, despite the outgoing prime minister publicly attacking Palestinian parties and accusing them of supporting terrorism. Abbas said Natan Eshel, Netanyahu's former chief of staff and longtime associate, approached him before and after last month's elections, seeking to establish whether his party would help opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot form a government. Speaking to Israeli public broadcaster Kan on Wednesday, Abbas confirmed an earlier Channel 12 investigation that revealed Eshel had repeatedly contacted him in an apparent attempt to discourage Ra'am from supporting Eisenkot. According to Abbas, Eshel wanted to know whether Ra'am would support legislation preventing politicians facing criminal indictments from serving as prime minister, a measure that could affect Netanyahu, who is standing trial on corruption charges. He also asked whether the Palestinian party would support efforts to establish an alternative government. Channel 12 reported on Monday that Eshel contacted Abbas several times before, during and after the 27 October elections. In one message sent after the results were announced, Eshel reportedly asked Abbas whether his party would help Eisenkot, despite the opposition leader's reluctance to include Ra'am in his coalition. Abbas did not respond to the later approaches, according to the report. Eshel initially denied conveying messages but subsequently acknowledged questioning Palestinian politicians about whether they had the self-respect to support a government that did not want them as coalition partners. Netanyahu's Likud party denied that the communications were authorised by the prime minister, saying he had been surprised to learn of them. The revelations have prompted accusations of hypocrisy against Netanyahu, who has repeatedly sought to delegitimise Palestinian parties as potential partners in an alternative government. During a speech to the newly elected Knesset on Tuesday, Netanyahu accused Palestinian lawmakers of supporting terrorism and seeking Israel's destruction. Abbas accused Netanyahu of exploiting his official position to incite against Palestinian citizens of Israel and their parliamentary representatives. He also warned that the prime minister's rhetoric had endangered both him and his family. Hamas designation controversy The revelations come as Abbas faces mounting pressure over reports that he might agree to designate Hamas a terrorist organisation in exchange for participation in an Eisenkot-led government. Israeli outlet Ynet reported on Tuesday that representatives of Eisenkot's Yashar party and Yair Golan's Democrats had been engaged in intensive discussions with Ra'am. According to the report, Abbas had indicated a willingness in principle to accept Eisenkot's demand that prospective coalition partners recognise Hamas as a terrorist organisation, provided Ra'am received a genuine role in government. However, Abbas rejected claims that he had made such a declaration during an interview with Arabic-language Hala TV on Wednesday. "I did not make this statement," he said, warning Palestinian citizens against relying on politically motivated reports attributed to unnamed sources. Abbas urged the public to recognise only official declarations issued directly by Ra'am or its representatives. His denial did not explicitly rule out making such a declaration during future coalition negotiations. Eisenkot has made recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organisation one of four conditions for participation in his prospective government, alongside recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and commitments concerning national service. Golan has acknowledged discussions with Ra'am, suggesting that the Hamas designation need not prevent Abbas from joining the coalition. However, Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party could be crucial to forming a government, remains opposed to an administration dependent on Ra'am or the Joint List. Eisenkot was tasked by President Isaac Herzog on Sunday with forming a government after Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority in the elections. Palestinian parties could prove decisive in determining whether Eisenkot succeeds, despite continued opposition from several Jewish parties to their direct participation in government. Abbas has insisted that Ra'am wants to become an influential coalition partner rather than simply provide parliamentary support for Netanyahu's removal.

pending.title: Israeli settlers injure Palestinians as army dismantles outposts
pending.summary: Israeli settlers stormed a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank and injured five people on Thursday, a rights group said, after the military dismantled illegal outposts. The Israeli military, which has come under international criticism over settler violence, said it intervened and took down two outposts built by settlers without permission. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements across the West Bank, all of which are deemed illegal under international law, and some of which, known as outposts, are built without Israeli government approval. "After Israeli military forces left the area, dozens of settlers, armed with clubs, tear gas and stones, stormed the village of Atara, " the Israeli rights group Yesh Din said in a statement. "Five residents were injured and hospitalised, one in serious condition with a brain hemorrhage," Yesh Din added. The Palestinian Red Crescent said one of the injured people was 67 years old. The army said it had removed tents, vehicles and "temporary structures" erected by settlers in two outposts including one near Atara. "During the enforcement activity near Atara, Israeli rioters barricaded themselves inside structures" and were dispersed, the military added. Abdelhadi Atari, a resident of Atara and local journalist, told AFP that settlers broke into and vandalised Palestinian houses soon after the army arrived. "The fact that the army had blocked the village from several directions (ahead of the dismantling operation) also helped the settlers attack and operate freely during the assault inside the village," Atari said. "The children were terrorised. The settlers ripped doors off houses. Some houses had their doors torn off, and all the windows were smashed," Atari added. Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967, with settlements there proliferating under caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government. Government ministers have stoked the escalating settler violence and called for the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the territory. The Israeli military frequently allows settlers to rampage in Palestinian villages unimpeded. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank since the 7 October 2023 attack by Gaza-based Hamas on Israel, mostly by Israeli soldiers but also by settlers, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry. More than 50 Israelis have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations over the same period, according to Israeli figures. A number of countries including Britain and France in September announced trade sanctions on products from settlements over the violence. France last week refused entry to Yossi Dagan, the head of a body representing Israeli settlements in the West Bank, according to his office. The Israeli foreign ministry highlighted the efforts to dismantle outposts, saying four were taken down over two days. "The law applies to everyone," it said on X. (AFP and TNA staff)

ready.title: Nine-month-old baby dies of cold in Gaza
ready.summary: A nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on Thursday, his father and a doctor told AFP , after days of harsh weather and flooding in the Gaza Strip that displaced thousands of Palestinians living in tents. The doctor, who saw the child and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq "died from hypothermia inside his family's displacement tent" in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip. Ahmed Raqiq, told AFP that his son Kinan died of cold during the night in their tent in southern Gaza. "I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser hospital , but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death," he said. "I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in burial shroud," he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet. Heavy rain last week flooded tens of thousands of people's tents in Gaza, where virtually the whole population has been displaced at least once by three years of Israeli strikes in response to the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas. Five people including three children died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment collapsed onto their tents. Rain and cold Since then, hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and central and northern areas of the territory after they were inundated by rainwater. James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN children's agency, UNICEF, warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season. "It's very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It's not yet winter," Elder said. "We're weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold." The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms. Around 65% of Gaza's people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said. Israel and Hamas declared a ceasefire on October 10, 2025 but Israel has kept striking the territory, vowing to kill anyone involved in the 7 October attack, the deadliest in Israel's history. In rare criticism, President Donald Trump's Board of Peace said this week that Israel - which tightly controls entry into Gaza - had not done enough in anticipation of the cold weather and that it needed urgently to let in more supplies. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a response to the Board of Peace, said that Israel had allowed in supplies including 91,000 tents and that "Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza". "Hamas must not be allowed to exploit humanitarian supplies and equipment to rebuild its terror capabilities," Netanyahu said. (AFP)

paras: یک نوزاد ۹ ماهه فلسطینی به نام «کینان احمد رقیق» در اثر سرمازدگی شدید داخل چادر آوارگان در خان‌یونس واقع در جنوب نوار غزه جان خود را از دست داد؛ پدر این کودک اعلام کرد پس از کبود شدن بدن فرزندش او را به بیمارستان ناصر منتقل کرده اما نوزاد بر اثر سرمازدگی پیش از رسیدن جان باخته بود.

این حادثه پس از بارندگی‌های سیل‌آسا رخ داد که موجب آب‌گرفتگی ده‌ها هزار چادر آوارگان در سراسر نوار غزه شده است؛ هم‌اکنون حدود ۶۵ درصد از مردم غزه در چادرهای موقت به سر می‌برند و آژانس‌های سازمان ملل از جمله یونیسف و اوچا نسبت به وقوع بحران جدی‌تر با آغاز فصل سرما هشدار داده‌اند.
